title: ¡Adiós, Cordera!
author: Leopoldo Alas "Clarín"

premise.en: In a green meadow in Asturias, two poor siblings and their beloved old cow watch the railway arrive — and learn, twice over, what a train can take away.
premise.es: En un prado verde de Asturias, dos hermanos pobres y su querida vaca vieja ven llegar el ferrocarril, y aprenden, dos veces, lo que un tren puede llevarse.

summary.en: Rosa and Pinín grow up in the meadow of Somonte with their father's old cow, Cordera, watching the new telegraph pole and the trains that pass nearby. When debts force their father to sell Cordera to be slaughtered, the children cry their farewell at the station. Years later, the same station and the same cry return under far graver circumstances.
summary.es: Rosa y Pinín crecen en el prado de Somonte junto a la vieja vaca de su padre, Cordera, observando el nuevo poste de telégrafo y los trenes que pasan cerca. Cuando las deudas obligan a su padre a vender a Cordera para el matadero, los niños gritan su despedida en la estación. Años después, la misma estación y el mismo grito regresan en circunstancias mucho más graves.

contentWarning: A beloved family cow is sold to be slaughtered, and a young man is conscripted and sent to war (mentioned in one sentence).

tutorNotes.pronunciation: This is a northern Spanish text; practice the crisp final -d in «adiós» and the diphthongs in «tierra» and «hierro», both frequent in the story's imagery.
tutorNotes.grammar: The narration mixes pretérito, imperfecto and pluscuamperfecto for the timeline, imperfect subjunctive after past-tense reporting verbs (suplicaron que no vendiera), conditional for hypothetical futures (subirían a un tren), and passive constructions (había sido comprada) — watch how these layer to build the story's sense of inevitability.
tutorNotes.culture: The arrival of the telegraph and railway in rural Asturias in the late nineteenth century symbolized a modernity that rarely benefited the peasants it passed through; military conscription by lottery (the quintas) fell hardest on poor families who could not pay for a substitute.
tutorNotes.commonErrors: Don't confuse «matadero» (slaughterhouse) with anything related to bullfighting; also note that «aldea» (small village) is smaller and more rural than «ciudad» or even «pueblo».
